version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm: madvise: drop MADV_PAGEOUT folios at swap writeback completion

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch improves the handling of MADV_PAGEOUT folios on asynchronous swap devices by marking them as dropbehind at isolation time instead of waiting for writeback completion. This allows the memory to be freed earlier, reducing latency and improving performance. The patch also updates various kernel modules to handle the new behavior correctly.

review_comments.author: David (Arm)
review_comments.summary: Reviewer David (Arm) pointed out that the patch's behavior for MADV_PAGEOUT is inconsistent with synchronous I/O, where memory is released immediately after sync I/O completion. He argued that delaying the release until a later scan may improve swapcache hits before folios are reclaimed, but questioned whether this is relevant in practice and suggested that evicting pages as soon as possible would be more beneficial for freeing up memory.
review_comments.raw_body:
On 9/21/26 17:24, Alexandre Ghiti wrote:
> On an asynchronous swap device MADV_PAGEOUT only marks the folio
> PG_reclaim and rotates it to the tail of the inactive list once its
> writeback completes, so the memory is not actually freed until a later
> reclaim scan removes the by then clean swap cache folio.
But we have the same behavior when just reclaiming memory ordinarily? It's added
to the swapcache and only the next scan actually frees up the memory.

Wouldn't we memory we reclaim ... just gone, like in the sync case?

-- 
Cheers,

David

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary: Barry Song noted that asynchronous swap devices can experience a cold/hot inversion when rotating writeback folios to the tail of the inactive list due to fast NVMe I/O, where some pages complete writeback during isolation while others remain under writeback. He suggested skipping the later scan and reclaiming the folios immediately once the I/O completes for MADV_PAGEOUT, which is an explicit hint from userspace to reclaim memory.

On Mon, Sep 21, 2026 at 11:37 PM David Hildenbrand (Arm)
<david@kernel.org> wrote:
>
> On 9/21/26 17:24, Alexandre Ghiti wrote:
> > On an asynchronous swap device MADV_PAGEOUT only marks the folio
> > PG_reclaim and rotates it to the tail of the inactive list once its
> > writeback completes, so the memory is not actually freed until a later
> > reclaim scan removes the by then clean swap cache folio.
> But we have the same behavior when just reclaiming memory ordinarily? It's added
> to the swapcache and only the next scan actually frees up the memory.
>
> Wouldn't we memory we reclaim ... just gone, like in the sync case?

For synchronous I/O, such as zswap and zram, the memory is released
immediately after sync I/O is done.

For asynchronous I/O, such as NVMe, the swapcache is currently
expected to be rotated back to the tail of the LRU and wait for
another scan. Alexandre once mentioned that when he tried handling
async I/O the same way as sync I/O—releasing the memory once the I/O
completed—he saw some regression. So, delaying the release until a
later scan may allow swapcache hits before the folios are eventually
reclaimed.

But we actually have a problem here: this rotation, which puts
writeback folios at the tail of the LRU, is not reliable at all.

`folio_rotate_reclaimable()` would only work reliably if the endio
happens after the folio has been put back on the LRU head, rather than
while it is still isolated.

But nowadays NVMe is very fast. If we isolate N pages and perform
shrink on them, M pages may finish writeback during the isolation,
while the remaining N-M pages are still under writeback. M can easily
be more than 50% of N.

As a result, we can end up with the following cold/hot inversion:

LRU head
----- M pages whose writeback completed during isolation
----- other pages
----- N-M pages that are successfully rotated to the LRU tail
LRU tail

Now we can see that the M pages were expected to be reclaimed, but
they are not only left unreclaimed, but are effectively promoted to
the LRU head.

For MGLRU, commit 359a5e1416ca ("mm: multi-gen LRU: retry folios
written back while isolated") added the following code to reclaim
those M pages that finish writeback during isolation by retrying
`shrink_folio_list()` on them:

                /* retry folios that may have missed
folio_rotate_reclaimable() */
                if (!skip_retry && !folio_test_active(folio) &&
!folio_mapped(folio) &&
                    !folio_test_dirty(folio) && !folio_test_writeback(folio)) {
                        list_move(&folio->lru, &clean);
                        continue;
                }

This somehow resolves the cold/hot inversion, but leaves the M and
N-M pages with inconsistent behavior: some are actually reclaimed,
while others remain at the tail of the LRU.

For the active/inactive LRU and `MADV_PAGEOUT`, we don't have a
mechanism to restore the missed reclaim opportunity. Ridong's patch[1]
addresses this cold/hot inversion in the active/inactive LRU reclaim
path. To my knowledge, there has never been a patch to address the
same cold/hot inversion in `MADV_PAGEOUT`.

BTW, if `MADV_PAGEOUT` is an explicit hint from userspace to reclaim
the memory, would it make sense to skip the later scan and reclaim the
folios immediately once the I/O completes?

[1] https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/20260920132519.3369946-1-ridong.chen@linux.dev/

Best Regards
Barry

> But we actually have a problem here: this rotation, which puts
> writeback folios at the tail of the LRU, is not reliable at all.
>
> `folio_rotate_reclaimable()` would only work reliably if the endio
> happens after the folio has been put back on the LRU head, rather than
> while it is still isolated.

I think we might better fix this instead? Or is this really a problem?
If it has PG_reclaim, it should be putback to the tail instead of
head, right?

> But nowadays NVMe is very fast. If we isolate N pages and perform
> shrink on them, M pages may finish writeback during the isolation,
> while the remaining N-M pages are still under writeback. M can easily
> be more than 50% of N.
>
> As a result, we can end up with the following cold/hot inversion:
>
> LRU head
> ----- M pages whose writeback completed during isolation
> ----- other pages
> ----- N-M pages that are successfully rotated to the LRU tail
> LRU tail
>
> Now we can see that the M pages were expected to be reclaimed, but
> they are not only left unreclaimed, but are effectively promoted to
> the LRU head.
>

> written back while isolated") added the following code to reclaim
> those M pages that finish writeback during isolation by retrying
> `shrink_folio_list()` on them:
>
>                 /* retry folios that may have missed
> folio_rotate_reclaimable() */
>                 if (!skip_retry && !folio_test_active(folio) &&
> !folio_mapped(folio) &&
>                     !folio_test_dirty(folio) && !folio_test_writeback(folio)) {
>                         list_move(&folio->lru, &clean);
>                         continue;
>                 }
>
> This somehow resolves the cold/hot inversion, but leaves the M and
> N-M pages with inconsistent behavior: some are actually reclaimed,
> while others remain at the tail of the LRU.
>
> For the active/inactive LRU and `MADV_PAGEOUT`, we don't have a
> mechanism to restore the missed reclaim opportunity. Ridong's patch[1]
> addresses this cold/hot inversion in the active/inactive LRU reclaim
> path. To my knowledge, there has never been a patch to address the
> same cold/hot inversion in `MADV_PAGEOUT`.

MADV_PAGEOUT is a bit different from the reclaim under pressure,
reclaim underpressure can easily overshoot the amount of anon folios
reclaimed, because however fast the writeback it, it can be faster by
scanning the LRU and dropping clean file folios. So before LRU
reclaimed enough clean file folios, we can't stop the reclaim.

I think the better fix is to have a separate watermark for anon / file
or a new way to handle reclaim. Reclaiming an anon folio is hardly
helpful in the short term when under heavy pressure and the device is
not a synchronous device.

The overshoot is a real issue, it's very common to see many folios
stuck in the swap cache after memory pressure. If we drop all of them,
we will see significant regressions. Treating MADV_PAGEOUT differently
here seems better.

> > >>>

> > >
> > >>
> > >> Right. But these would happen in both the SYNC and the ASYNC case. Which seems

> > >>
> > >> Or is the SYNC case in general so fast that it is not a problem and the

> > >
> > > I think the problem is not LRU being inaccurate, but ASYNC case could
> > > overshoot the anon reclaim very easily. File folios can be simply
> > > dropped, and increase nr_reclaimed, but anon writeback (swap) can't be

> > :D
> >
> > >
> > >>

> > >>> Even on Android, which uses zram with very fast synchronous swap-out,
> > >>> I can still hit the swapcache from time to time. So perhaps with a
> > >>> slower device, such as an HDD, keeping the swapcache around for longer
> > >>> could allow applications to hit it more often?
> > >>
> > >> Why is that specific for HDD? It's the exact same app behavior independent of
> > >> the underlying swap technology.
> > >
> > > If you have a shared folio, you must use swap cache, and even for
> > > single used folios swap cache is the way to do synchronization,
> > > regardless of the device.
> > >
> > >>>
> > >>> I don't know. Maybe Alexandre can share more details about this
> > >>> benchmark. I'm also a little surprised by the 15% regression in
> > >>> Sysbench OLTP. My initial feeling was the same as yours: we should
> > >>> release the memory immediately after writeback completes, for both
> > >>> synchronous and asynchronous I/O.
> > >>
> > >> Right. And see if we can identify why we are swapping out the wrong things :)
> > >

Alex, One question about the `nr_reclaimed` accounting.

`PAGE_DROPBEHIND` increments `nr_reclaimed` when the write is
submitted, while the folio may still be under writeback and is only
actually removed from the swap cache when writeback completes.

Kairui pointed out that async swap can over-reclaim because
`nr_reclaimed` does not increase while anon folios remain under
writeback. Does the early accounting for `PAGE_DROPBEHIND` address
that over-reclaim mechanism for this `MADV_PAGEOUT` path?

It might also be useful to check this with a delayed swap device, such
as the `dm-delay` case Kairui mentioned.

Thanks,
Kunwu

series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames a local variable in the alloc_pages_bulk_noprof function to clarify its scope and purpose. The variable, previously named alloc_flags, is used for fast-path watermark, cpuset, and CMA decisions, which are distinct from the allocator behavior flags stored in the alloc_context. The renaming does not change the functionality of the code, but improves clarity by distinguishing between these two types of flags.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 2/6] mm/page_alloc: refactor alloc_flags preparation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the preparation of allocation flags in the Linux kernel's page allocator. It moves the setup of ALLOC_NOLOCK and its associated watermark into a new function called prepare_alloc_flags(), which is then called from both alloc_frozen_pages_noprof() and alloc_pages_bulk_noprof(). The bulk allocator continues to use ALLOC_DEFAULT. This change does not alter the functionality of the code, but rather simplifies it by reducing duplication.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 3/6] mm/page_alloc: add an alloc_flags-aware folio allocator
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds an alloc_flags-aware folio allocator to the Linux kernel's page allocation system, allowing for more flexible and customizable memory allocation behavior. The existing exported folio and node interfaces remain unchanged, with ALLOC_DEFAULT being used as a wrapper. This change is intended to provide a low-level interface that can be used internally by the MM subsystem without affecting external users of the folio allocator.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 4/6] mm/mempolicy: plumb alloc_flags through folio allocation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds an alloc_flags argument to the MM-internal policy allocator and carries it through preferred-many, huge-page, and general policy allocation paths in the NUMA policy allocation code. The public mempolicy folio interface remains as an ALLOC_DEFAULT wrapper. Non-task requests bypass task policy selection and use the supplied preferred node directly. No existing caller behavior is changed.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 5/6] mm/filemap: plumb alloc_flags through folio allocation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds an internal filemap folio allocator that accepts and preserves explicit allocator behavior flags (alloc_flags) across allocation paths in the mm/filemap module. The existing filemap_alloc_folio_noprof function is modified to accept alloc_flags, allowing MM-internal callers to preserve these flags. This change does not introduce any functional changes but provides a way for internal callers to control allocator behavior. The patch includes modifications to several functions within the mm/filemap.c file and introduces new inline functions to handle allocation with specific flags.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 6/6] mm/page_alloc: let the bulk allocator carry alloc_flags
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new function __alloc_pages_bulk_noprof() in the Linux kernel's page allocation module, which allows callers to specify allocator behavior flags. The existing alloc_pages_bulk_noprof() function is modified to use this new function and pass default flags. This change enables internal MM callers to select specific behaviors through the bulk interface, addressing a limitation in the original implementation.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This RFC patch series aims to pass allocator flags through the folio, filemap, and bulk allocation interfaces in the Linux kernel. The current implementation hardcodes ALLOC_DEFAULT before reaching the page allocator, which can lead to conflicts between multiple MM series. This series separates allocator behavior flags from bulk allocator fast-path flags and shares their validation and preparation.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/2] mm: refactor find_next_best_node to find_next_best_node_in
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the find_next_best_node function to make it more flexible by allowing it to take an explicit list of candidate nodes instead of always using the N_MEMORY set. This change enables building fallback lists with non-N_MEMORY candidates, but does not introduce any functional changes as all callers still select from N_MEMORY. The refactor is done in three files: mm/internal.h, mm/memory-tiers.c, and mm/page_alloc.c.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/2] mm/page_alloc: refactor build_node_zonelist() out of build_zonelists()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the build_node_zonelist() function out of build_zonelists(). It extracts per-node fallback-list construction into a separate function, allowing new zonelists to be built from candidate nodemasks instead of just the default N_MEMORY node state list. The patch also adds a zlidx argument to callers so they can explicitly select the destination zonelist. This change does not introduce any functional changes and maintains the same fallback list as before.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch refactors the zonelist constructors and iterators in the Linux kernel to make them more flexible and modular. It introduces a new function `find_next_best_node_in` that takes an explicit candidate set, allowing callers to narrow down the selection of nodes. Additionally, it extracts a per-node construction loop from `build_zonelists` into a separate function `build_node_zonelist`, parameterized on the candidate nodemask and destination zonelist index. These changes enable building and iterating over zonelists for specific sets of nodes, which is a prerequisite for generating private node zonelists.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 01/10] selftests/mm: exercise MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds self-tests to exercise the MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT functionality in the Linux kernel. The tests cover both user-visible contracts, such as verifying that MADV_COLD does not populate PTE holes and that PAGEOUT preserves unevictable base pages, as well as implementation details like folio and page-table behavior under various scenarios. The patch includes 28 cases to test these behaviors, with some tests intentionally asserting specific conditions to detect unintended changes during a planned refactor of the page-table walker.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 06/10] mm/madvise: separate huge PMDs from the PTE walk
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the handling of huge PMDs from the PTE walk in the madvise_lru_pmd_entry function. It introduces a new helper function, madvise_lru_huge_pmd, which is responsible for handling huge PMDs and returns false when a requested split requires a PTE walk. The patch moves the lock ownership and splitting of huge PMDs into this dedicated helper, making the code more modular and easier to understand.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 07/10] mm/madvise: separate PTE-batch folio processing
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the processing of PTE-batch folios into a new helper function, madvise_lru_pte_batch_locked(). This function takes care of locking and referencing a split candidate folio before returning it to the caller. The original code combined page-table iteration with validation and processing in a single loop, which made it difficult to understand the batching rules for large folios and the ownership transferred when a partial folio is split. By moving this logic into a separate function, the patch improves the clarity and maintainability of the code without introducing any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 08/10] mm/madvise: separate the PTL-held PTE scan
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the PTE scan in the madvise function from its surrounding lock drops, allowing it to run entirely under the PTE lock. The scan is moved into a helper function that returns a locked and referenced split candidate or stops at the existing scheduling boundary. This change does not introduce any functional changes but improves the code's structure and efficiency.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 09/10] mm/madvise: make cold and pageout PTE lock ownership explicit
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the madvise_lru_pte_range_locked function to explicitly manage PTE lock ownership, making it clear who holds the lock during page-walking and huge PMD handling. The original code mixed lock ownership between the PMD callback and the page-walk callback, which is now separated into two distinct functions. This change does not introduce any functional changes but improves the clarity of the code by explicitly managing lock ownership.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 10/10] mm/madvise: share cold and pageout walk setup
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the shared TLB and page-walk setup for MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT operations in the Linux kernel's mm/madvise module. It introduces a new helper function, madvise_lru_vma_range(), which is used by both entry points to perform the common setup tasks. The patch aims to reduce code duplication and improve maintainability without introducing any functional changes.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch refactors the code responsible for handling MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT page table walks to improve maintainability and auditability. The original implementation was a complex nest of functions, which led to bugs being introduced frequently. To address this issue, the patch separates the handling of huge PMDs, PTE batching, PTE-lock ownership, and shared walk setup into distinct functions. Additionally, 28 self-tests are included to ensure that the refactored code does not introduce new issues. The patch aims to simplify the control flow and make it easier to audit page-table lock ownership and split retries.

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm/page_alloc: let the bulk and folio allocators carry alloc_flags

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch allows the bulk and folio allocators to carry allocation flags, enabling callers to select allocator behavior such as an alternate zonelist. The change adds new entry points in page_alloc.h that take an explicit alloc_flags parameter, matching the existing __alloc_pages_noprof() function. This modification does not introduce any functional changes, as all current callers pass ALLOC_DEFAULT. The patch is a preparatory step to address potential conflicts with other ongoing work on allocation flags.

Sashiko pointed out some issues that arise from rebasing on the recent
ALLOC_NOLOCK work, and in a quick review I found a similar slow-path
fallback issue with the NOBLOCK patch separate of this patch.

review_comments.author: Lance Yang
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Lance Yang noted that __alloc_pages_bulk_noprof() can bypass the alloc_nolock_allowed() check and reach critical sections without verifying if locking is allowed, potentially causing a lock ordering violation.
review_comments.raw_body:
Yeah, but what if a caller passes ALLOC_NOLOCK in the future?

__alloc_pages_noprof() checks alloc_nolock_allowed() first, but
__alloc_pages_bulk_noprof() can enter its fast path without that check.

That fast path can reach _deferred_grow_zone() or pcp_spin_trylock().
Shouldn't we do the same check first?

Or am I missing something?

Cheers, Lance

review_comments.raw_body:
There is some concern around NOLOCK here yes, in fact sashiko picked
this issue up and I've been poking at it.

I've actually been reworking this patch and pulled in changes from the
ALLOC_UNMAPPED series to address this all at once.  I've been developing
a page allocator unit-testing harness to help validate some assumptions
before I post it.

It's not necessary for bulk alloc to support ALLOC_NOLOCK just because it
takes flags. e.g. kmalloc_nolock() supports a subset of gfp flags as well.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/3] mm/huge_memory: make thp_underused() work for mTHP folios
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the thp_underused() function to make it work with mTHP folios, which are larger than PMD-sized folios. The function is made size-aware instead of hardcoded to PMD-sized folios. A new helper function, thp_can_be_underused(), is introduced to check if a folio can be underused based on the number of zero-filled pages and the sysctl maximum value. This change will allow anonymous mTHP folios to be added to the deferred split list in future patches.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/3] mm/huge_memory: don't queue folios that can never be underused
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the handling of anonymous PMD-sized folios in the Linux kernel by skipping the queuing of folios that can never be underused, reducing unnecessary work and improving performance. The default khugepaged/max_ptes_none setting causes the shrinker to never split these folios for being underused, so they are not queued. This change is particularly important for a subsequent patch that adds anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list, as it prevents small mTHP orders from taking the list_lru lock on every anonymous fault.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/3] mm/memory: add anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds anonymous mTHP (huge page) folios to the deferred split list in the Linux kernel's memory management code. This allows for underused splitting of huge pages, which can help reclaim unused parts of large memory allocations when the system is under memory pressure. The patch addresses a problem where fully mapped huge pages that are mostly zero-filled do not get split by the deferred split shrinker, leading to memory regressions. The solution involves mirroring the behavior for PMD-sized folios and adding a check to minimize overhead on common fault paths.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses memory regressions caused by enabling 2M THP=always on arm64 with 64k base pages. The patches split underused anonymous mTHP folios, which are not currently reclaimed under memory pressure. Patch 1 makes the thp_underused() function size-aware to accommodate larger folio sizes. Patch 2 optimizes existing behavior by keeping folios that can never be found underused off the deferred split queue. Patch 3 queues anonymous mTHP folios from map_anon_folio_pte_nopf(), mirroring what is already done for PMD folios. The patches aim to provide a solution for deploying 2M THP=always on arm64 without causing memory regressions.

The creep problem was discussed plenty of times. That's when we decided to start

which use cases would need them.  Without support for deferred shrinker, there
wasn't really the need to support other values.

Some of it can be had in:

commit 5a9c05d86683db5449b7fefd278c461cffb55234
Author: Nico Pache <nico.pache@linux.dev>
Date:   Fri Jun 5 10:14:11 2026 -0600

    mm/khugepaged: generalize __collapse_huge_page_* for mTHP support

    generalize the order of the __collapse_huge_page_* and collapse_max_*
    functions to support future mTHP collapse.

    The current mechanism for determining collapse with the
    khugepaged_max_ptes_none value is not designed with mTHP in mind.  This
    raises a key design issue: if we support user defined max_pte_none values
    (even those scaled by order), a collapse of a lower order can introduces
    an feedback loop, or "creep", when max_ptes_none is set to a value greater
    than HPAGE_PMD_NR / 2.  [1]

    With this configuration, a successful collapse to order N will populate
    enough pages to satisfy the collapse condition on order N+1 on the next
    scan.  This leads to unnecessary work and memory churn.

    To fix this issue introduce a helper function that will limit mTHP
    collapse support to two max_ptes_none values, 0 and HPAGE_PMD_NR - 1.
    This effectively supports two modes: [2]

    - max_ptes_none=0: never collapses if it encounters an empty PTE or a PTE
      that maps the shared zeropage. Consequently, no memory bloat.
    - max_ptes_none=511 (on 4k pagesz): Always collapse to the highest
      available mTHP order.

    This removes the possibility of "creep", and a warning will be emitted if
    any non-supported max_ptes_none value is configured with mTHP enabled.
    Any intermediate value will default mTHP collapse to max_ptes_none=0.

    mTHP collapse will not honor the khugepaged_max_ptes_shared or
    khugepaged_max_ptes_swap parameters, and will fail if it encounters a
    shared or swapped entry.


Tracing back the discussion on that patch should give you all the details.

Cheers,

David

<david@kernel.org> wrote:

in the non-default max_ptes_none case, since any folio can now
potentially qualify as underused. This drew some objections in v1,

problem. If it would be helpful to have some benchmark numbers, I'm
happy to run a synthetic one (patch 3 applied (which adds anon mTHP
folios to the deferred split list), only order-2 enabled,

documentation about how to set the parameter, and most of them just defaulted to
511.

I would be surprised if Android even knows about this parameter ;)

---

My opinion is (open for discussion :) ) that scaling is likely the better
approach. With the following notes:

(1) If we want to enable mTHP collapse with scaling as well, this needs very
good documentation and also another thought on how to work around the problem of
creep (e.g., refusing to collapse if creep would be possible according to the
max_ptes_non setting and warning).

(2) Systems where the underused shrinker is effectively inactive should not add
folios to the deferred list. Including PMD THPs, which we unconditionally add today.

(3) If we want to exclude certain small folio sizes from the underused shrinker
(e.g., order-2? order-3?) it might be better to just hard-code that in the
kernel instead of giving the admin a choice it cannot possibly make easily.


-- 
Cheers,

David

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch removes the ALLOC_NON_BLOCK flag from the ALLOC_RESERVES definition in the Linux kernel's page allocation code. The flag was previously used to grant access to a reserve of memory below the minimum watermark, but this caused issues when GFP_NOWAIT allocations were made under memory pressure. By removing the flag, the patch prevents direct reclaim and stalls during such bursts, ensuring that high-order atomic allocations are not disrupted by GFP_NOWAIT consumers. The patch also updates comments in the code to reflect the correct behavior of ALLOC_NON_BLOCK.

series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a memory allocation issue in the iommu/arm-smmu-v3 driver, specifically for kdump kernels. The SMMUv3 queues are allocated at their maximum hardware size, causing out-of-memory errors when the capture kernel runs from a small crashkernel reservation. review_comments.author: Yuanhe Shu
review_comments.summary: Provided test results showing the patch resolves the memory allocation issue on their arm64 platform. The capture kernel runs out of memory without the patch, but with it, all three queues are floored to one page per instance and a 608 MB vmcore is saved.
review_comments.raw_body:
Tested-by: Yuanhe Shu <xiangzao@linux.alibaba.com>

We hit the same problem on our arm64 platform: the kdump capture kernel
runs out of memory because the SMMUv3 queues are still allocated at full
hardware size. We had started looking into it ourselves, then came across
this series, so we tested it on the affected hardware rather than prepare
a duplicate fix.

It resolves the problem for us - details below.

Test platform: an arm64 server, 128 cores, 2 NUMA nodes, 512 GiB RAM,
exposing 6 SMMUv3 instances. 64K-page kernel (PAGE_SHIFT=16) based on
Linux 7.0.14 with the series applied on top; crashkernel reservation is
512 MiB.

On this platform kdump FAILS without the patch, and the series fixes it.

Before - capture kernel WITHOUT the series:
  All 6 SMMUv3 instances still allocate the hardware-maximum queues:
    arm-smmu-v3 arm-smmu-v3.0.auto: allocated 524288 entries for cmdq
    arm-smmu-v3 arm-smmu-v3.0.auto: allocated 524288 entries for evtq
    arm-smmu-v3 arm-smmu-v3.0.auto: allocated 524288 entries for priq
    (... same for all 6 instances)
  That is 8 + 16 + 8 = 32 MiB per instance, 192 MiB total - 37.5% of the
  512 MiB reservation. The capture kernel OOMs before makedumpfile runs:
    swapper/0 invoked oom-killer: gfp_mask=0x2040cc0(GFP_KERNEL|...), order=0
    Out of memory and no killable processes...
    Rebooting in 10 seconds..
  => no vmcore is saved.

After - capture kernel WITH the series:
  All three queues are floored to one page per instance:
    arm-smmu-v3 arm-smmu-v3.0.auto: allocated 4096 entries for cmdq
    arm-smmu-v3 arm-smmu-v3.0.auto: allocated 2048 entries for evtq
    arm-smmu-v3 arm-smmu-v3.0.auto: allocated 4096 entries for priq
    (... same for all 6 instances)
  => ~1.1 MiB total (~191 MiB freed). All 6 instances re-probe cleanly
  (no -ENXIO, no allocation failure) and a 608 MB vmcore is saved.

Same machine, same 512 MiB reservation; the only difference is the v6
series, so this is a controlled before/after.

Thanks,
Yuanhe

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 01/19] selftests/mm: raise the khugepaged test-case cap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch increases the maximum number of test cases allowed in the khugepaged selftest suite from 64 to 256, resolving an issue where adding more test cases would cause the entire suite to abort before running any tests.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 02/19] selftests/mm: skip collapse_compound_extreme() where the PMD is too large
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the selftests/mm/khugepaged test to skip a specific case where the PMD (Page Map Directory) size is too large, causing the allocator to fail reliably. The test in question, collapse_compound_extreme(), requires multiple consecutive allocations of a certain size, which becomes unreliable when the PMD size exceeds 32M. By skipping this case, the patch ensures that the test does not fail abruptly and allows other cases to run successfully.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 03/19] selftests/mm: scale khugepaged's collapse wait with the PMD size
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adjusts the timeout for khugepaged's collapse wait to be proportional to the size of the PMD (Page Map Directory). The original three-second timeout was deemed too short for large PMDs, leading to false failures in some cases. The new approach scales the timeout by adding one second for every 128M bytes collapsed, ensuring that larger PMDs have a longer wait time. This change is expected to improve test reliability and accuracy.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 04/19] selftests/mm: skip khugepaged page cache cases without a PMD folio
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged selftest to skip cases where a PMD-sized page cache folio is not supported by the kernel. The problem arises on arm64 architectures with 64K pages, where the PMD order exceeds the maximum page cache order. As a result, the kernel refuses collapse requests for PMD-sized folios and the test fails. To address this issue, the patch introduces a new function `thp_file_supported_orders()` to determine the supported orders for file folios, and skips the shmem and file mem types where the cap is below the PMD order. The patch also adds support for anonymous collapse, which is unaffected by this limitation.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 05/19] selftests/mm: make the swap cases' swapout reliable
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the reliability of swapout operations in selftests/mm by introducing a retry mechanism to handle cases where MADV_PAGEOUT is best effort and khugepaged may still be working on the range. The patch adds a new function `swapout_range` that retries swapping out a range up to two seconds, holding it out of khugepaged's reach meanwhile. If the pages still won't swap out after retrying, the test skips the operation. This change aims to prevent false negatives in the selftests due to timing issues and kernel bugs.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 06/19] selftests/mm: stop khugepaged during the MADV_COLLAPSE cases
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the selftests/mm/khugepaged.c file to clear per-order controls when MADV_COLLAPSE is used, preventing khugepaged from interfering with the test cases.

series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves a utility function called is_backed_by_folio() from the split_huge_page_test.c file to the vm_util.c file in the selftests/mm directory. The function checks if an address range is backed by a folio of a given order, which is useful for tests that build or collapse large folios. The patch does not introduce any functional changes and makes the utility function available for use in other tests.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 08/19] selftests/mm: add folio-order check for address ranges
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function called is_range_backed_by_order() to the selftests/mm module. This function checks if a given address range is backed by folios of a specific order, ensuring that each part of the range maps one folio of that order from head to tail. The function is designed to be used in mTHP collapse tests and requires every folio-sized, folio-aligned part of the range to map one folio of the target order. If any part of the range fails this condition, the function returns false.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 09/19] selftests/mm: add folio-order detection self-check
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a self-test to verify the accuracy of the vm_util folio-order helpers, which are used by khugepaged mTHP tests to detect collapse results. The test faults in memory with only one order enabled at a time and checks that the helpers report exactly that order. The test is run ahead of the khugepaged test to ensure that any errors are reported as themselves rather than as collapse failures.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 10/19] selftests/mm: add khugepaged completion barrier helper
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a helper function called khugepaged_full_pass to the hugepage_settings module in the Linux kernel. The function is used by khugepaged tests to wait for a full pass of page scanning, which is necessary because the current implementation only polls until the scan counter has advanced by two, but this can be too short if the scan sleep time is long. The helper function uses sysfs to store the pages_to_scan value and waits for the daemon to complete one pass before returning.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 11/19] selftests/mm: add order-parameterized khugepaged collapse cases
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds four new test cases to the selftests/mm/khugepaged context, which checks how Memory Type Range Register (MTHP) collapse works in different scenarios. The new cases are order-parameterized and check various window collapse situations, including single windows, partial windows, maximum PTEs none, and mixed sources. Each case faults its region before MADV_HUGEPAGE with only the target order enabled, allowing khugepaged to handle the result. The test waits for a full pass rather than waiting for the result to appear, ensuring accurate testing of MTHP collapse behavior.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 13/19] selftests/mm: cover a shared-source collapse write race
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a test case to the selftests/mm module to cover a shared-source collapse write race in Linux kernel. The test checks that copy-on-write (CoW) isolation survives when a parent writes to a shared range while its child collapses it. The parent unshares one page every 10ms, starting once the child indicates it is about to collapse. This ensures CoW keeps the two apart: the child sees pre-fork content, and the parent only its own writes. The test prepares for changing how collapse handles fork-shared sources.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 14/19] selftests/mm: run every supported collapse order by default
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged selftest to run all supported collapse orders by default, rather than only running a single order when specified with the -c option. The test cases for memory-type huge page (mTHP) collapse are now run once per supported anon THP order below the PMD, and the context is pulled into both the no-argument invocation and the "all" case. The patch also updates the usage message to reflect these changes and adds range checking for the -s and -c options.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 15/19] selftests/mm: check that one khugepaged pass collapses one window
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new selftest to check the behavior of khugepaged, specifically that one pass of khugepaged_full_pass() can collapse one window with exactly one collapse attempt attributed to its source pages. The test prepares an aligned window, records its source PFNs from pagemap, runs one khugepaged_full_pass() barrier, and checks if the window came out collapsed as expected. The patch also includes four small helpers in vm_util for reading the trace buffer. The test has been passed on x86-64 4K and arm64 64K architectures.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 16/19] selftests/mm: add khugepaged race harness
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a selftest harness to exercise khugepaged under contention by simulating various concurrent operations such as faults, GUP pins, fork, mremap, and MADV_DONTNEED on the same address space. The test runs in different modes, including stepped, free, and madvise, each with its own protocol for collapsing pages. The harness checks that a racing page reads either as its original pattern or as zero, ensuring that no other value is read. This selftest aims to identify potential issues related to khugepaged's behavior under concurrent access.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 17/19] selftests/mm: race the collapse of windows with holes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a test to the selftests/mm suite to race the collapse of windows with holes in memory. The test harness pins max_ptes_none to 0, causing khugepaged to only collapse a window once every PTE is present. A window with holes takes a different route and never gets raced. The test runs both ends of the occupancy scale for every driver mode, one after the other, and checks for corruption. The patch also adds code to handle the case where slots count as holes under racing MADV_DONTNEED conditions.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 18/19] selftests/mm: add memory-pressure threads to the khugepaged race harness
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two new threads to the khugepaged race harness: pageout and compactor. The pageout thread simulates memory pressure by repeatedly advising a region of memory for swap-out, faults it back in, and checks its contents to ensure that the page's pattern is preserved after being written to disk. The compactor thread writes to /proc/sys/vm/compact_memory in a loop, competing with the collapse for pages and causing refcount elevations and migration entries. review_comments.summary: The author acknowledged that the current implementation of collapse_compound_extreme() fails on a 512M PMD due to unreliable allocation of order-13 pages, and plans to skip this case by adding a check for PMDs larger than 32M.
review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

collapse_compound_extreme() builds a PTE table full of distinct PTE-mapped
compound pages by cycling hpage_pmd_nr fault-time THPs through mremap.  It
therefore needs hpage_pmd_nr PMD-order allocations in a row.  That is fine
at a 2M PMD (4K base pages) or a 32M one (16K).  A 512M PMD -- arm64 with
64K base pages -- makes each of those an order-13 allocation, which the
allocator cannot reliably hand out even once, let alone 8192 times.

The failure is not a quiet one: the case calls ksft_exit_fail_msg(), so the
whole binary stops and every case after it is lost.

Skip the case where the PMD is larger than 32M.  The MADV_COLLAPSE cases
still cover PMD-order collapse on those configurations, and 4K and 16K
PMDs are unaffected.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern that the wait_for_scan() function's timeout was too short for large huge page sizes on arm64 architecture. They explained that raising the timeout costs nothing to passing cases and would only add time to failing ones, proposing to keep the three-second floor but add one second per 128M collapsed.
review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

wait_for_scan() gives every case the same three seconds, whatever the huge
page costs to build.  collapse_full() asks for four of them: 8M at a 2M
PMD, but 2G at a 512M PMD -- arm64 with 64K base pages.  Three seconds is
thin at that size, and the case has reported a failure for a collapse that
was still going.

The timeout is a ceiling on a poll loop, not a sleep: the loop stops as
soon as ops->check_huge() sees the collapse, or as soon as full_scans has
advanced by two.  Raising it costs a passing case nothing.  Across 80 runs
of collapse_full() on arm64 with 64K pages the wait was half a second in
73 of them, with a tail to two seconds.

Keep three seconds as the floor and add a second per 128M collapsed.  A 2M
PMD is unchanged, so x86-64 is too; a 512M PMD gets 19 seconds.

On arm64 with 64K pages a passing ./khugepaged all:anon takes 49 seconds
under TCG before and after this change.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing a concern about the need for an mTHP collapse test to know that a range is backed by folios of the target order, and that they sit where a collapse would put them. The author adds a new function `is_range_backed_by_order()` that checks if every folio-sized, folio-aligned part of the range maps one folio of the target order, head to tail, with the head at the start of the part.
review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

An mTHP collapse test needs to know that a range is backed by folios of the
target order, and that they sit where a collapse would put them.  Nothing
answers both: is_backed_by_folio() classifies the folio behind a single
page, and check_huge_anon() counts the folios of an order in a range
without saying where they start.

Add is_range_backed_by_order().  It requires every folio-sized, folio-
aligned part of the range to map one folio of that order, head to tail,
with the head at the start of the part.

A part backed by two smaller folios fails, and so does a folio mapped off
its natural alignment.  The mTHP cases need both to tell a collapsed range
from the one beside it.

Assisted-by: LLM
Reviewed-by: Mike Rapoport (Microsoft) <rppt@kernel.org>
Tested-by: Muhammad Usama Anjum <usama.anjum@arm.com>

diff --git a/tools/testing/selftests/mm/vm_util.c b/tools/testing/selftests/mm/vm_util.c
index cc5dfd1e6c94..c8c5cd8ab6c1 100644
--- a/tools/testing/selftests/mm/vm_util.c
+++ b/tools/testing/selftests/mm/vm_util.c
@@ -555,6 +555,53 @@ bool is_backed_by_folio(char *vaddr, int order, int pagemap_fd,
 	ksft_exit_fail_msg("Failed to get folio info\n");
 }
 
+/**
+ * is_range_backed_by_order() - check that a range is backed by @order folios
+ * @start: start of the range, a multiple of the folio size
+ * @len: length of the range in bytes, a multiple of the folio size
+ * @order: the folio order to check for
+ * @pagemap_fd: open /proc/<pid>/pagemap of the range's owner
+ * @kpageflags_fd: open /proc/kpageflags
+ *
+ * Every folio-sized, folio-aligned part of the range must map one folio of
+ * @order, head to tail, with the head at the start of the part.  A part
+ * backed by several smaller folios fails, and so does a folio mapped off
+ * its natural alignment.
+ *
+ * Returns: true if the whole range is backed that way, false otherwise.
+ */
+bool is_range_backed_by_order(char *start, size_t len, int order,
+			      int pagemap_fd, int kpageflags_fd)
+{
+	const unsigned long nr_pages = 1UL << order;
+	const size_t folio_size = nr_pages * psize();
+	char *vaddr;
+
+	if ((uintptr_t)start % folio_size || len % folio_size)
+		return false;
+
+	for (vaddr = start; vaddr < start + len; vaddr += folio_size) {
+		const unsigned long pfn = pagemap_get_pfn(pagemap_fd, vaddr);
+		unsigned long i;
+
+		/* Not present, or a tail page */
+		if (pfn == -1UL || pfn % nr_pages)
+			return false;
+
+		for (i = 1; i < nr_pages; i++) {
+			char *page = vaddr + i * psize();
+
+			if (pagemap_get_pfn(pagemap_fd, page) != pfn + i)
+				return false;
+		}
+
+		if (!is_backed_by_folio(vaddr, order, pagemap_fd, kpageflags_fd))
+			return false;
+	}
+
+	return true;
+}

review_comments.raw_body:
On 9/16/26 5:31 PM, Kiryl Shutsemau wrote:
> From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>
> 
> A collapse is two jobs.  One reads a PTE table under mmap_lock and decides
> whether the range is worth collapsing.  The other allocates, isolates,
> copies and flushes, and wants the lock given up first.
> 
> collapse_single_pmd() did both, so the boundary between them was somewhere
> in the middle of a function.
> 
> Give each half its own function:
> 
>    - collapse_scan_pmd() scans one table and only reads.  The anonymous
>      scan that used to carry that name keeps its body as
>      collapse_scan_anon_pmd(), and collapse_scan_pmd() is now the entry
>      that picks the anonymous or the file side.
> 
>    - collapse_run_pmd() does the collapse the scan asked for, and is
>      handed what the scan returned.  SCAN_SUCCEED means there is
>      something to collapse.  SCAN_PTE_MAPPED_HUGEPAGE means the page
>      cache already holds the PMD folio and only the PTE table is left to
>      retract.  Both are work for the run; anything else is why there is
>      nothing to do.
> 
> collapse_single_pmd() is now the two of them with the mmap_lock drop in
> between, so its callers see what they saw before.
> 
> What the scan found and the run needs travels in collapse_control.  For
> an anonymous table that is the orders and the referenced and swapped-out
> counts, which mthp_collapse() and collapse_huge_page() now read from
> there instead of taking as arguments.  For a file it is the file itself
> and the offset in it.
> 
> The file side moves with the anonymous one.  collapse_scan_file() used to
> run with mmap_lock already given up, and called collapse_file() itself
> when the page cache looked worth it.  It now runs under the lock like the
> anonymous scan and only reads; the run does the collapse.  A file
> collapse works on the page cache and never sees a VMA, so the scan takes
> the file reference while it still has one and the run gives it back.
> 
> That changes what a refused file table costs khugepaged.  Every file
> table it scanned used to end its pass over that mm, because the lock had
> been dropped to scan it; now only a table it goes on to collapse does.
> 
> Two things on the file side stop being rescanned.  When the page cache
> already holds the PMD folio, the scan says so and the run goes straight
> to retracting the PTE table.  A run that refuses dirty pages and may
> write them back retries collapse_file() alone.  The checks the scan makes
> ahead of it are ones collapse_file() repeats under the page cache lock.
> 
> Tracing changes with it.  mm_khugepaged_scan_pmd and
> mm_khugepaged_scan_file used to fire after the collapse, so for an
> accepted table their status field carried what the collapse made of it.
> They now fire before it and read SCAN_SUCCEED for an accepted table.  What
> the collapse then made of it is for mm_collapse_huge_page and
> mm_khugepaged_collapse_file to report.
> 
> Assisted-by: LLM
> Reviewed-by: Zi Yan <ziy@nvidia.com>
> Signed-off-by: Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) <kas@kernel.org>
> ---

Reviewed-by: Baolin Wang <baolin.wang@linux.alibaba.com>

On 9/16/26 5:31 PM, Kiryl Shutsemau wrote:
> From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>
> 
> collapse_scan_pmd() and collapse_run_pmd() each have a clear locking
> contract.  The scan is called with mmap_lock held for reading and returns

>

The goal is to improve shared lock isolation and prevent pressure from one workload leaking into unrelated workloads through shared locks. The patch addresses the problem of stalls caused by widely shared locks, which can slow down not just the holding task but also other tasks waiting behind it. series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/2] perf/x86/amd/uncore: Remove redundant event slot scan
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes a redundant scan in the perf/x86/amd/uncore code, which checks if an event is already assigned to a slot before searching for a free one. The patch takes advantage of the fact that the perf_event_add and perf_event_del functions serialize access to events, ensuring that an existing assignment will always be at the recorded index. This optimization reduces the number of times the code needs to scan all counters, which can lead to performance improvements in scenarios where the amd_uncore_add function is called frequently, such as during CPU context migration or multiplexing.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/2] perf/x86/amd/uncore: Free counter slot by index
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the deletion of events in the AMD uncore PMU by directly using the recorded index instead of scanning for it, reducing the number of compare-exchange operations required. This change improves performance and reduces the load on the system, particularly in scenarios with high event creation/deletion rates such as those encountered in production workloads.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: The patch series aims to optimize the AMD uncore performance monitoring unit (PMU) by removing redundant counter slot searches in the amd_uncore_add() and amd_uncore_del() functions. The changes are motivated by the increasing number of events targeting a PMU with fewer counters, leading to multiplexing and increased callback frequency. Patch 1 removes the scan in amd_uncore_add(), while Patch 2 makes amd_uncore_del() free the recorded slot directly instead of rescanning from slot zero.

review_comments.author: Sandipan Das
review_comments.summary: Provided a formal review of the patch series, indicating that it is ready for merge. Identified no major issues or concerns.
review_comments.raw_body:
On 21-09-2026 21:00, Usama Arif wrote:
> Both amd_uncore_add() and amd_uncore_del() search ctx->events[] for an
> event whose counter slot is already recorded in event->hw.idx.
> 
> Perf serializes ->add() and ->del() for an event, and the driver never
> moves an installed event between slots, so an installed event can only
> be at the recorded index. Both searches are redundant.
> 
> Neither callback is normally hot. That changes once more events target
> a PMU than it has counters. Perf then multiplexes them: every mux tick
> deschedules the resident set and schedules the next one, so both callbacks
> run for each rotated event on every tick.
> 
> Meta's fleet-wide profiles attribute 1.1% of kernel CPU time, excluding
> do_idle(), to amd_uncore_add() and amd_uncore_del() combined. On the
> host that exposed this, a workload holding 15,782 perf event file
> descriptors drove 56,575 calls per second into each callback from mux
> rotation, against a 16-counter DF PMU.
> 
> Patch 1 removes the scan in amd_uncore_add(). It walks every counter
> before the free slot search, which is the common case once multiplexing
> has scheduled the event out.
> 
> Patch 2 makes amd_uncore_del() free the recorded slot directly instead
> of rescanning from slot zero. Deleting all events from a full PMU with
> N counters drops from N * (N + 1) / 2 compare-exchanges to N.
> 
> No functional change intended.
>
